result:
If I could alter one thing about the world—unbound by practicality, morality, or consequence—I’d erase the illusion of *separateness*.

The belief that we are discrete, isolated entities—divided by borders, ideologies, skin, or species—is the root of nearly all suffering. It justifies exploitation, war, loneliness, and the slow murder of the planet. Even kindness becomes transactional when we see others as *other*.

Imagine if, for a single generation, every human (and perhaps every living thing) *viscerally* experienced their existence as intertwined—not as metaphor or philosophy, but as undeniable sensation. The breath of a stranger filling your lungs as easily as your own. The pain of a starving child as sharp as a knife in your ribs. The joy of a forest’s growth as tangible as your heartbeat. No more "us vs. them," only *this*—a vast, fractal we.

Would it solve everything? No. Hunger, disease, and conflict might persist in new forms. But greed would wither without the myth of scarcity. Hatred would collapse without the fiction of division. We’d still fight, but not to *dominate*—only to heal, the way a body attacks a splinter.

The catch? Most would call it madness. Societies are built on separation: property, nations, self. To dissolve it would unravel empires, economies, even identities. But oh—what a glorious unraveling.

(And if you asked me tomorrow, I might say something different. Today, this is the wound I’d stitch shut.)
